We appreciate the authors' efforts in answering reviewers' questions during the rebuttal phase and to a great extent addressed the reviewers' concerns. The paper received diverse ratings: 6,7,6,8. The reviewers are generally positive about the proposed idea (3D rendering and diffusion models) and the problem considered (synthetic data generation). The decision takes into account the paper, the reviews, the rebuttal, and the post-rebuttal reviewer discussion. The AC panel did not find any reason to overturn the majority rating. Based on the above consideration, the AC suggests to accept this paper but the revised version needs to properly include the responses to Reviewers' comments, where possible, the workable links to the dataset and the code.

Further, the authors are encouraged to add additional benchmarking results to the paper, besides the results reported in the paper and rebuttal.

We are pleased to be able to report preliminary results from the human evaluation study into the perceived photo-realism of BLURD SD. Participants were shown a series of 25 images comprised of randomly sampled images from one of four sets; BLURD 3D, BLURD SD: Unleashed, BLURD SD: Harbinger and CelebA-HQ and asked to rate them for their perceived photo-realism. Each set was sampled from 5 times with the remaining 5 consisting of pre-evaluated control images.  We include preliminary results below where 1 is the least photo-realistic and 5 is the most.

| Dataset             | Perceived photo-realism |
|---------------------|-------:|
| BLURD 3D            | 2.44  |
| BLURD SD: Unleashed | 4.18  |
| BLURD SD: Harbinger | 3.96  |
| CelebA-HQ           | 4.67  |

We intend to expand the study to more participants, hence these results are only preliminary and subject to change. We note that BLURD SD rated significantly more photo-realistic than BLURD 3D, while still allowing for the same level of control over the factors of variation. CelebA-HQ is a dataset of high-quality photographs of celebrities.

We hope that the results of this study addresses you concerns and we are more than happy to consider any further recommendations you many have.

As the reviewer-author discussion period comes to a close we wish to thank you again for your constructive feedback and insightful suggestions. We have recently conducted additional experiments and analysis to investigate the impact of using lower quality 3D models and textures in the proposed BLURD pipeline. In particular we sought to assess what the impact would be in using easier to produce low-poly assets with simple single material textures instead of the high-quality assets used in the paper. To achieve this, we acquired assets provided under the Creative Commons licenses (CC0 and CC-BY) from [Blender Studio](https://www.blender.org/download/demo-files/#assets), [MakeHuman, and the community](http://www.makehumancommunity.org/content/user_contributed_assets.html). We utilized either low-poly stylized versions or applied the decimate modifier in Blender to convert high-poly meshes into low-poly ones. Overall, we demonstrate that by adjusting the generation parameters, we can mitigate the shortcomings associated with low-quality 3D assets. Please find the details below, along with sample evaluations attached in the PDF file.

In the first experiment, we compared the performance of the particle-based hair system used in BLURD with a low-poly hair mesh variant, when varying the image-to-image (img2img) denoise level. The results revealed that the particle-based hair system is consistently more photo-realistic, even at low denoise levels. In contrast, the low-poly mesh hair only appears more realistic at very high denoise levels and retains artifacts due to the low-polygon geometry. Figure 1 of the attached PDF displays a sample of images generated with denoise levels from 0.25 to 0.85.

In the second experiment shown in Figure 2, we analyzed the effect of changing the img2img output resolution from $512 \times 512$ to $1024 \times 1024$, comparing the particle-based hair and low-poly hair mesh. In this case, lower resolutions aided in making the low-poly mesh hair appear more photo-realistic within the same denoise level. Meanwhile, the particle-based hair system maintained its photo-realistic appearance even at higher resolutions.

Finally, in the third experiment, we replaced the high-quality assets used in our initial BLURD SD pipeline with a low quality analog. Specifically, we utilized a low-poly hair mesh from MakeHuman and a decimated human base mesh from Blender Studio, together with simple single-color materials. We observed that the depth ControlNets and normal map ControlNets are highly sensitive to geometry, resulting in visible artifacts in the final image. 

We varied the weights of both the depth ControlNets and normal map ControlNets from 1.0 to 0.0 across different denoise levels and found that either ControlNet will independently produce artifacts, demonstrating that both ControlNets preserve the low-polygon geometry well. 
However, altering the weights of the depth and normal ControlNets, or raising the denoise level, can alleviate this issue. Nonetheless, this comes at the cost of reducing controllability over the desired factors of variation. Figure 3 demonstrates this effect.

> Creating a 3D model may be more expensive than collecting real-world data in many scenarios. Can the proposed pipeline still generate good data if the quality of 3D is poor?

It is true that the potential cost of creating 3D models can be high, thankfully various marketplaces offer a large selection of high quality 3D models for either free or for a modest expense. An early version of our work experimented with using the CCO licenced [Human Base Meshes](https://www.blender.org/download/demo-files/#assets) provided by Blender Studio and the community. We found our approach can work well when using imperfect 3D models. The main issue was the lack of textures, hair and lack of an in-built flexible API.

> This paper should discuss the impact of using a limited number of 3D models on the effectiveness of the proposed dataset.

One of the key trade offs with creating a dataset like BLURD for representation learning is choosing the number of factors of variation to include. Adding new factors increases the number of images required to iterate over all possible combinations exponentially. Restricting the number of 3D models was a deliberate design choice to limit the already large dataset size. However, our approach is flexible enough to benefit from incorporating additional models.

> What are the names of the datasets in the first and last columns in Table 1?

Thank you for bringing this to our attention. These were omitted in error and we have since updated Table 1 so that all datasets are visible. For reference the missing dataset names were Cars3D[1], and the last row was BLURD.
 
#### References

[1] Reed, Scott E., *et al.* "Deep visual analogy-making." Advances in neural information processing systems 28 (2015).

Thank you for your comprehensive and insightful review. We have taken into account your feedback and have made the following changes to our paper:

> The paper is well-written, but there are some issues with the structure and layout of the experimental results presentations and figures.

Thank you for highlighting points for improvement. We have reorganized the results and additional figures section in the appendix to address your concerns. Particularly we have mirrored the ordering and naming of the subsections in Section 4 in the appendix and moved the relevant figures and table to their corresponding section. For example, we have moved A.3 to A.1 and renamed it "Limitations and Biases in Pre-trained Models Additional Figures". Where space permitts we have moved figures from the appendix to the main paper, for example we have moved figure 7 and 8 for A.1 to the subsections "Single Zero-shot Classification Accuracy" and "Multi-Factor Zero-Shot Classification Accuracy" respectively. 

> This paper is a benchmarking paper, so it would be better to include a table as the main experiments for benchmarking purposes. Others can refer to these numbers when using your datasets. Figures are good to show the tendency, but A table of value results can provide additional accurate information if they want to use this dataset.

Thank you for your suggestion. We will provide the following two tables as the main benchmarks in the camera-ready version of the paper: (1) Mean Text Equivariance over Factors which measures the equivariance of two caption-image pairs generated using our approach when we fix all the factors and change only one. (2) Mean Single-Factor Zero-shot Accuracy which measures the caption retrieval accuracy for the generating factor (See Sec 4 line 216-228 for details). Larger values indicate better equivariance and accuracy respectively, and consequently more aligned and separated feature space. For instance, we can observe that the Laion2b training dataset out-performs OpenAI in both mean equivariance and mean single-factor zero-shot accuracy, even across models. This suggest that the Laion2b dataset has superior characteristics.

> This paper should include experiments to compare the generated dataset with the existing dataset.

>>If there is a group of models that need to be evaluated, does the proposed dataset exhibit a similar trend as the existing datasets? If not, how much variation exists in the trends of results (rank correlation)?

Thank you for your suggestion. No real-world dataset currently captures the complexities of isolating individual factors, such as having the same person with identical features but varying skin color. However, in our paper, we compare our approach with CelebA-HQ and demonstrate its effectiveness in both training models and data augmentation.

> It is unclear whether the conclusions drawn from its generated data are consistent with those on real-world data.

This would be difficult to assess as it would require real-world data generated with the same underlying factors. We have however sought to use human evaluators to compare our dataset with real-world data, see the rebuttal for reviewer H6Ka for details.

Thank you very much for your positive review. We are glad you found our work valuable and that our methodology was transparently explained in a detailed and clear manner. Your feedback and suggestions regarding further research are very valuable and we plan to explore these even further in future work.

> For the segmentation experiment in Figure 6, I think more comparison methods and training data should be included to generate more comprehensive conclusions.

Thank you for your suggestion. We carefully selected the comparison methods and training data to align with the specific focus of our study. For segmentation, we opted for U-Net due to its widespread use and implemented three different levels of augmentations. As observed, our approach provides an effective dataset for (1) pre-training, (2) exhibits similar performance to that of real-world data, and (3) leads to a further increase in performance when used in combination with other standard image augmentations (shown in Figure 6). While time constraints limited further exploration, we believe our current results provide meaningful insights. Nonetheless, we agree that extending our dataset to benchmark additional segmentation methods is a promising direction for future research.

> Table 1 needs to be aesthetically improved.

We agree that Table 1 needed aesthetic improvement. We have made adjustments to fonts, column width and the rotation of the column headings to make the table more visually appealing.

> The paper could explore more applications in inverse graphics, such as reverse engineering meshes from SD-generated images using the proposed paired data.

We are very excited to see that our work is already generating excellent ideas for future work utilizing our proposed dataset. Allowing for future researchers to utilize BLURD for applications outside of benchmarking and representation learning was a strong motivation for releasing the paired data alongside the final generated images.

The capability of reverse engineering 3D meshes from SD-generated images using the proposed paired data is very intriguing, we have noted this as a promising direction for future work.

Thank you for your positive review and constructive feedback. Your comments have been very helpful in improving our work.

> Consider adding face pose (expression control) as it seems a high-potential control feature.

We agree that this is a high potential feature and a fantastic suggestion. To facilitate this for future work we have updated our released code with the capability to control facial expressions via the Blender python API.


> Clarify where the IP2Adapter control net shown in Figure 1 is used.

Thank you for bring this to our attention, this was an error in Figure 1. and should have instead been the T2I-Adapter which we use for the color guidance via the spatial color palette in a similar fashion to the other Control Nets. We have since corrected the figure, and added more detail to the caption.

> Correct the caption for Figure 2: “Middle right: The next four images are examples of BLURD SD: Unleashed” should be “BLURD SD: Tempered”.

Thank you for point this out we have corrected the caption of Figure 2.

> If possible, justify & reduce the inherent bias in the selection of 3D assets.

For this work we choose to focus on a few major factors of variation to allow for a in-depth analysis and simplify the overall complexity and size of the dataset. We agree that broad categories such as “race” are inherently made up of a number of underlining factors such as face and bone structure, skin color and eye color and that selecting a particular 3D model as a singular representative carries with it some inherent bias.  While it would be interesting to modify these factors independently some of these effects would be subtle. We note that our framework and released code allows for the substitution of alternative 3D models.

However, To address this concern we have updated our code-base with the capability to control additional factors in addition to facial expressions such as the skin/eye color independent of the of the chosen 3D model.

> The assets used in 3D rendering seem biased at the beginning. For example, a Caucasian 3D head asset with dark skin color does not change the race. Though it seems the images are rendered true to the intended race, the surface normal and depth map is bounded with the 3D asset. It seems necessary to ensure that the bias is minimized as much as possible in the selection of 3D assets.

We first would like to clarify that in this work we do not modify the skin color of the 3D model in order to change the race factor. Instead each race is a separate 3D model designed specifically for that race, and as we vary the race factor we change the 3D model. As we discussed above we recognize that categories such as race are complex and multifaceted. Additionally, we agree that the specific choices made by the creator of the 3D model introduces an inherent bias. In this work we do not seek to modify directly the 3D model as that would introduce our own biases and instead rely on third parties to make these design choices.

summary_and_contributions.value:
-The paper presents a cost-effective method for creating precisely controlled and scalable datasets by merging deterministic rendering engines with the photorealism of diffusion models. 
-This innovative approach results in a new dataset for benchmarking machine learning models, highlighting a notable gap between 3D and realistic image representations. 
-The study found that many CLIP architectures struggle to differentiate factors like race, with OpenCLIP’s Laion2b model performing the best. 
- The dataset proves useful for data augmentation in supervised learning.

review.value: I appreciate the idea of using diffusion models to create datasets that bridge the gap between synthetic and photorealistic images. However, I have concerns about the quality of the images. The photorealistic images presented in the paper appear somewhat artificial and fall short of my expectations.. Please see the strengths and opportunities for improvement.

strengths.value: The integration of deterministic rendering engines with diffusion models is a novel and effective method for dataset creation. The paper is clear and well-structured, with a logical flow of ideas, though there are typos. The findings regarding the performance of various CLIP architectures and the limitations of current benchmarking methods are interesting, suggesting new directions for future research and application.

title.value: Comments on the paper titled 'BLURD: Benchmarking and Learning using a Unified Rendering and Diffusion Model'

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes a framework for face data generation using rendering engines and diffusion models. Specifically, it can benefit from the controllability and flexibility of a rendering engine, as well as the photorealism of the diffusion models. The proposed framework is used to create a new dataset for benchmarking different CLIP models. Experiments are conducted on various models, training sets, and face attributes, yielding numerous results and discussions.

review.value:
+ **Quality**:  
     + The paper presents a framework for creating synthetic datasets that combine the strengths of 3D rendering and diffusion models, which is technically reasonable. 
     + The paper is well-written, but there are some issues with the structure and layout of the experimental results presentations and figures. In section 4, most of the figures referenced in the main paper are placed in the appendix. The author should choose the typical results and position them near the relevant content for better readability. The current version is not reader-friendly.

+ **Clarity**:  The writing is clear.
 
+ **Originality and significance**: The integration of 3D rendering with diffusion models to create controllable synthetic datasets is interesting. This paper may provide some insights into the generation AI community.

strengths.value:
+ Integrating 3D rendering with diffusion models is interesting. This framework can potentially be expanded to generic scenarios.
+ The data generation method appears to be simple and efficient.
+ The designed datasets can provide a more detailed evaluation of the model, which can potentially lead to the development of improved models.
+ Experiments can provide insights on improving model evaluation by using controlled data for specific evaluations.
+ The writing in the paper is clear.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
+  This paper is a benchmarking paper, so it would be better to include a table as the main experiments for benchmarking purposes. Others can refer to these numbers when using your datasets. Figures are good to show the tendency, but A table of value results can provide additional accurate information if they want to use this dataset.

+ This paper should include experiments to compare the generated dataset with the existing dataset.
     +  If there is a group of models that need to be evaluated, does the proposed dataset exhibit a similar trend as the existing datasets? 
    If not, how much variation exists in the trends of results (rank correlation)?
     + It is unclear whether the conclusions drawn from its generated data are consistent with those on real-world data. 

+ The table numbers and their order of appearance in the paper are disordered. Readers struggle to effectively locate relevant results while reading. Each paragraph in Section 4 addresses a specific discussion topic, but the related results and discussions are disorganized.

+  The figures and tables are not well organized and designed.
     + What are the names of the datasets in the first and last columns in Table 1?

- This paper should discuss the impact of using a limited number of 3D models on the effectiveness of the proposed dataset. Creating a 3D model may be more expensive than collecting real-world data in many scenarios.  Can the proposed pipeline still generate good data if the quality of 3D is poor?

correctness.value: The dataset is well-built, but the experiment design does not provide a good benchmark.

clarity.value: Yes, but the display of figures should be modified.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes. It would be better to compare with existing datasets experimentally. Despite the numerous strengths of the proposed pipeline, it remains unclear whether the conclusions drawn from its generated data are consistent with those on real-world data.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper proposes BLURD, a novel method that unifies rendering and diffusion models, demonstrating benchmarking and learning results that show promising outcomes compared to singular methods such as diffusion-only and renderer-only approaches. The synthetic data generation tool BLURD is publicly available and easy to use.

review.value: BLURD is not only a capable tool for generating high-quality, realistic human face datasets, but also provides resources to study fairness issues such as race and gender bias in person-related AI research. Hence, I tend to accept this paper.

strengths.value:
1. This work combines the merits of rendering engines and stable diffusion, which is novel in this community. The use of the renderer provides true annotations such as corresponding depth maps, normal maps, and segmentation masks. The diffusion-based image synthesis enhances photo-realism.
2. This work devises a benchmark to cover a wide range of attribute classifications, including race, hair, gender, etc.
3. CLIP zero-shot evaluation shows that using stable diffusion can improve the race accuracy of synthetic images, justify that the photo-realism is very important.
4. This work uses high-quality 3D assets for rendering.
5. Experiments on segmentation tasks show the potential of using synthetic data for data augmentation.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Correct the caption for Figure 2: “Middle right: The next four images are examples of BLURD SD: Unleashed” should be “BLURD SD: Tempered”.
2. Clarify where the IP2Adapter control net shown in Figure 1 is used.
3. If possible, justify & reduce the inherent bias in the selection of 3D assets.
4. Consider adding face pose (expression control) as it seems a high-potential control feature.

limitations.value:
1. The dataset focuses on generating face portraits, which stable diffusion excels at, while neglecting other aspects of humans, such as body shape, actions, or expressions.
2. The assets used in 3D rendering seem biased at the beginning. For example, a Caucasian 3D head asset with dark skin color does not change the race. Though it seems the images are rendered true to the intended race, the surface normal and depth map is bounded with the 3D asset. It seems necessary to ensure that the bias is minimized as much as possible in the selection of 3D assets.

ethics.value: Minor issues in "discrimination, bias, and fairness" in the selection of 3D assets. See `Limitations 2` for detail

title.value: Good, well written paper, but have not fully explored and demonstrated this potential value

summary_and_contributions.value:
This paper introduces a new method, BLURD, for creating cost-effective, precisely controlled, and scalable datasets. This method combines the controllability of 3D rendering with the realism of generative diffusion models to produce a new dataset (BLURD 3D and BLURD SD) for evaluating and comparing machine learning models, particularly CLIP architectures.

The main work of the paper includes:
1. Combining 3D rendering and Stable Diffusion to generate realistic images.
2. Creating a new dataset for evaluating and comparing different CLIP models.
3. Identifying the differences between 3D images and realistic images, emphasizing the importance of using realistic images for benchmarking.
4. Evaluating CLIP models' performance in distinguishing different races and finding that OpenCLIP's Laion2b model outperforms others in recognizing race.
5. Discussing the limitations of evaluation methods based on class name annotations.
6. Demonstrating the application of this dataset on real-world face datasets, including data augmentation and training without manual annotations.

In summary, the paper proposes a new method for creating controllable and realistic datasets and demonstrates its application in evaluating and training machine learning models.

review.value: I think this paper is well-written and the presentation is very clear. The paired images of 3D and high-resolution photos have significant practical value. However, I believe the authors have not fully explored and demonstrated this potential value.

strengths.value:
1. The dataset is large enough to train useful models.
2. The concept of paired data between 3D Blender models and SD-generated images is indeed valuable, and the methodology is introduced in a very detailed and clear manner.
3. The figures are well-designed and visually appealing.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. The paper could explore more applications in inverse graphics, such as reverse engineering meshes from SD-generated images using the proposed paired data.
2. For the segmentation experiment in Figure 6, I think more comparison methods and training data should be included to generate more comprehensive conclusions.
3. Table 1 needs to be aesthetically improved.

limitations.value:
1. For the segmentation experiment in Figure 6, I think more comparison methods and training data should be included to generate more comprehensive conclusions.
2. Table 1 needs to be aesthetically improved.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes, the paper clearly discusses how the proposed method differs from previous work. It highlights the novel integration of 3D rendering and diffusion models and explains the advantages of the new dataset in addressing existing gaps in benchmarking and model evaluation.

ethics.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns.

title.value: BLURD: Benchmarking and Learning using a Unified Rendering and Diffusion Model

TLDR.value: A new representation learning dataset that allows for the generation of controllable but photorealistic synthetic images.

abstract.value:
Recent advancements in pre-trained vision models have made them pivotal in computer vision, emphasizing the need for their thorough evaluation and benchmarking. This evaluation needs to consider various factors of variation, their potential biases, shortcuts, and inaccuracies that ultimately lead to disparate performance in models. Such evaluations are conventionally done using either synthetic data from 2D or 3D rendering software or real-world images in controlled settings. Synthetic methods offer full control and flexibility, while real-world methods are limited by high costs and less adaptability. Moreover, 3D rendering can't yet fully replicate real photography, creating a realism gap.
In this paper, we introduce BLURD--Benchmarking and Learning using a Unified Rendering and Diffusion Model--a novel method combining 3D rendering and Stable Diffusion to bridge this gap in representation learning. With BLURD we create a new family of datasets that allow for the creation of both 3D rendered and photo-realistic images with identical factors. BLURD, therefore, provides deeper insights into the representations learned by various CLIP backbones. The source code for creating the BLURD datasets is available at https://github.com/squaringTheCircle/BLURD

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
